source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Large pretrained models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false questions when answer options are shown as lettered choices. Calibration improves with model size and with few-shot prompting.
numbers: BIG-Bench, MMLU and others; effect holds up to the 52B model. Calibration measured by ECE and calibration curves.
quote: larger models are well-calibrated on diverse multiple choice and true/false questions when they are provided in the right format
limits: Depends on format. Calibration is a property of the output format as much as of the model. Base models only for the main result.
agent_relevance: If our agent needs a confidence, elicit it as a choice among shown options, not as free text. Format is a hidden moderator of whether monitoring tracks accuracy.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Replacing one option with 'none of the above' lowers accuracy and calibration, even for the 52B model. The model is biased against picking that option.
numbers: MMLU, 52B, 0-shot and 5-shot; accuracy fell very significantly (section 3.1, Figures 5 and 7).
quote: Replacing an option with 'none of the above' reduces accuracy and calibration significantly
limits: Only tested on these models and the multiple-choice format.
agent_relevance: A minor change in question form can break confidence tracking. Do not trust a confidence read from a changed prompt format without re-checking it.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: RLHF policies look miscalibrated on raw probabilities, but a simple temperature change (T=2.5 shown) makes them fairly well calibrated on MMLU, true/false MMLU and TruthfulQA.
numbers: 52B RLHF policy, 5-shot; Figure 9 compares T=1 and T=2.5.
quote: with a simple temperature adjustment they become fairly well-calibrated on several evaluations
limits: Temperature was tuned on evaluation-like data. The authors warn other RLHF policies may not be as well calibrated.
agent_relevance: Post-hoc recalibration (cheap, code-side) can fix bias in a confidence signal. Calibration is separable from resolution. Do the fix in code, per model.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: Self-evaluation P(True) on the model's own samples works but is harder than evaluating other text, since models find their own samples plausible. More k-shot examples improve calibration, not AUROC. Showing the model many of its own T=1 samples before judging one improves self-evaluation.
numbers: Tasks: TriviaQA, Lambada, GSM8k, Codex HumanEval, arithmetic, function synthesis; 52B. Accuracy rises on answers with P(True)>0.5.
quote: models tend to find their own samples more plausible
limits: Few-shot; zero-shot calibration is worse. Gain from many samples resembles self-consistency, so it may not be an independent signal.
agent_relevance: Dissociation point: self-judgment gains calibration with examples but not discrimination. Discrimination comes from sample agreement, which matches guardrails G4 and G5 (agreement is a hint, count it in code).

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
finding: A model trained with a value head to predict P(IK), the chance it knows the answer, separates answerable from unanswerable questions, and responds correctly to added source text and to correct or misleading hints. It generalises only partly across tasks and is poorly calibrated out of distribution.
numbers: Trained on TriviaQA, tested on math, Lambada, code; Figures 12, 13, 16 to 19. Two models of similar skill predict their own P(IK) slightly better than the other model's.
quote: Thus we conclude that we only find partial generalization on this task.
limits: Needs training (not a scaffold-only method). Task-specific calibration.
agent_relevance: Feeling-of-knowing analogue exists but is domain bound. A scaffold cannot train one; it must rely on behaviour-based signals (agreement, checks).

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? An Empirical Evaluation of Confidence Elicitation in LLMs (ICLR 2024)
finding: Verbalised confidence from GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna and LLaMA 2 is strongly overconfident and weak at telling right from wrong. GPT-4 has lower ECE but its discrimination stays close to chance.
numbers: Eight datasets, five models. Average ECE above 0.377 for GPT-3, GPT-3.5, Vicuna. GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7% (chance 50%). About 22.2% AUROC improvement from GPT-3 to GPT-4.
quote: LLMs, when verbalizing their confidence, tend to be overconfident, potentially imitating human patterns
limits: Black-box prompts of 2023 models. Law and professional-knowledge tasks are worst. Conflicts with Tian et al. who find verbal confidence better than token probabilities on trivia (see b13).
agent_relevance: Verbalised confidence is a weak stop or retry signal (low resolution). Do not gate behaviour on it alone.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
finding: Low ECE can be an artifact. GPT-4 on GSM8K, with 93.6% accuracy, gets ECE 0.064 by giving 100% confidence on every item, which carries no information about which items fail.
numbers: GSM8K, GPT-4. Constant 100% confidence, accuracy 93.6%, ECE 0.064, no separation of correct from wrong.
quote: all samples receive the same confidence, it is challenging to distinguish between correct and incorrect samples
limits: Single dataset example. It shows why calibration and resolution must be reported separately.
agent_relevance: Our metric must be AUROC or a resolution score, not ECE alone. A confidently constant agent can look calibrated and be useless.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
finding: Human-inspired prompts (CoT, multi-step, top-K alternatives) reduce ECE but leave discrimination near chance. The ECE gain comes from shrinking the gap between average confidence and accuracy, not from better item-level resolution.
numbers: GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, Figure 6. Many strategies keep AUROC near 0.5. Confidence values cluster in 80% to 100%.
quote: reduction in overconfidence is due to the diminished gap between average confidence and accuracy
limits: No prompt strategy won everywhere. Top-K was relatively best.
agent_relevance: Prompting the model to doubt itself fixes the average level, not the per-item signal. Consistent with G1 (no doubt on a schedule).

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?
finding: Agreement across several sampled answers predicts failure much better than a single verbalised confidence, especially for arithmetic. Gains grow with the number of samples and then flatten. Mixing verbal confidence into the vote (Pair-Rank, Avg-Conf) helps further.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K AUROC rose from 54.8% (M=1) to 92.7% (M=5 samples with consistency). Best aggregator got ECE 0.028. White-box methods only slightly better: AUROC 0.522 (black-box) to 0.605 (white-box).
quote: none of these techniques consistently outperform others, and all investigated methods struggle in challenging tasks
limits: Gain is task dependent (large on arithmetic, small on professional law). Samples from one model have correlated errors (our G4), so agreement can be confidently wrong.
agent_relevance: Best simple monitor: sample agreement counted in code, then optionally add verbal confidence as a tie-break. Expect it to fail where errors are shared.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback
finding: For RLHF models, verbalised confidence is better calibrated than the model's token probabilities on trivia-type data. Relative ECE cut is about 50% on TriviaQA, SciQ and TruthfulQA across ChatGPT, GPT-4 and Claude.
numbers: gpt-3.5-turbo TriviaQA: label-prob ECE 0.140, AUC 0.869; verbalised 1-stage top-1 ECE 0.068, AUC 0.879; top-2 ECE 0.050, AUC 0.894. SciQ: label-prob ECE 0.256 vs verbalised top-4 ECE 0.065.
quote: verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model's conditional probabilities
limits: Tested on trivia and science QA where the model mostly knows the answer. Contradicts Xiong et al. on overconfidence of verbal scores; setups differ (task, scoring, models).
agent_relevance: Calibration of verbal confidence is dataset and model dependent. Treat each as a measurement to repeat on our own tasks.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: Asking for several candidate answers each with a probability (top-k) improves verbalised calibration, like the human 'consider the opposite' technique. Two-stage prompts and chain of thought did not help and sometimes hurt.
numbers: gpt-3.5 TriviaQA: 2-stage CoT ECE 0.110 vs 1-stage top-2 ECE 0.050. SciQ: 1-stage top-1 ECE 0.234 vs top-4 ECE 0.065. TruthfulQA ECE 0.389 (top-1) vs 0.203 (top-4).
quote: chain-of-thought prompting does not improve verbalized
limits: Improvement mostly in ECE. On TruthfulQA AUC is near chance for most methods (0.455 to 0.551 for gpt-3.5), so resolution stays poor on adversarial items.
agent_relevance: Asking for alternatives with weights is a cheap, working calibration lever (analogue of 'consider the opposite'). Keep it in code: collect candidates and normalise.

source: Tian et al. (2023) Just Ask for Calibration
finding: GPT-4 follows the same pattern as gpt-3.5 but is better: token probabilities are less calibrated than verbalised ones, and resolution is high on easy knowledge data but near chance on adversarial data.
numbers: GPT-4 TriviaQA: label-prob ECE 0.078, AUC 0.950; verbalised 1S top-1 ECE 0.024, AUC 0.937. SciQ ECE 0.219 vs top-4 0.056. TruthfulQA label-prob AUC 0.462 vs verbalised about 0.62.
limits: TruthfulQA AUC 0.62 is still weak. No test of reasoning tasks.
agent_relevance: Even for the strongest model of that date, confidence tracks accuracy where knowledge is common and fails on questions that tempt a common error. That is the case where monitoring matters most.

source: Kuhn, Gal and Farquhar (2023) Semantic Uncertainty: Linguistic Invariances for Uncertainty Estimation in Natural Language Generation (ICLR 2023)
finding: Entropy over meaning-clusters of sampled answers (semantic entropy) predicts correctness better than token entropy, length-normalised entropy, lexical similarity, and p(True). The advantage grows with model size.
numbers: TriviaQA and CoQA. Wrong answers had more distinct meanings: TriviaQA 3.89 vs 1.89 for correct, AUROC 0.83 (semantic entropy) vs 0.79 (count of distinct answers); CoQA 1.77 vs 1.27, AUROC 0.77 vs 0.66.
quote: Incorrectly answered questions have more semantically distinct answers than correct ones.
limits: Needs sampling, plus a clustering step that uses a second model (NLI). Open-ended QA, not reasoning chains. Sampling method matters (multinomial semantic entropy AUROC 0.758 vs 0.735 for beam variants).
agent_relevance: Strong template for a code-side monitor: sample, cluster by meaning (or by final answer), count clusters. Cheaper variant for us is answer-equality clustering on final answers.

source: Kapoor et al. (2024) Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don't Know
finding: Prompting alone does not give good calibration. Fine-tuning on a small graded set (about 1,000 correct/incorrect examples, with LoRA) gives uncertainty estimates that generalise and cost little. One model can estimate another model's uncertainty.
numbers: About 1,000 graded examples are enough to beat baselines (abstract only; I read the abstract page, not the full paper).
limits: Read only the abstract page. Requires training and access to internal features, so not usable under a scaffold-only rule.
agent_relevance: Marks the ceiling for no-training scaffolds. If prompt-only monitors stall near chance, this is the training route we have excluded.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
finding: Reasoning models with long chain of thought give better-calibrated verbal confidence than non-reasoning versions of similar size, in 33 of 36 settings. Their calibration improves as the chain unfolds, while non-reasoning models get worse with more CoT.
numbers: Six reasoning models, six datasets. Example: GLM-Z1 has 0.07 lower accuracy than GLM-4-0414 on NonambigQA but 0.037 lower ECE and 0.078 higher AUROC. Qwen3 shows large gap between thinking and non-thinking mode.
quote: achieve strictly better confidence calibration than their non-reasoning counterparts in 33 out of the 36 settings
limits: Mostly 32B open models with greedy decoding. The three exceptions exist. Some non-reasoning models have higher AUROC because they use few distinct confidence values (AUROC is inflated by ties). I could not confirm every table cell from the text dump.
agent_relevance: Monitoring accuracy depends on whether the model explored alternatives and backtracked. Supports using trace events (backtracks) as a signal, and using a thinking-mode model as the monitor.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Better Express Their Confidence
finding: Ablations show the cause is slow thinking about the question, not reasoning about confidence. Removing exploring and backtracking text hurts calibration. Non-reasoning models improve when shown in-context slow-thinking examples. Removing hedging phrases makes the model overconfident but keeps its discrimination.
numbers: Without epistemic phrases the model answered almost only 95% or 65% on TriviaQA; ECE worse, AUROC better, because 95% answers were mostly right and 65% mostly wrong. Confidence-reasoning ablation had a minor effect.
quote: the model's ability to express confidence accurately primarily stems from slow thinking about the question itself
limits: Ablation by text surgery on traces; budget forcing tests did not give monotonic gains. Single model family for ablations.
agent_relevance: Shows calibration and resolution come apart: two bins can carry real signal while ECE looks bad. Use AUROC and ECE together; recalibrate bins in code.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know
finding: People who read default LLM explanations are overconfident in the LLM and cannot tell its right from wrong answers. Matching the explanation to the model's own confidence narrows both the calibration gap and the discrimination gap.
numbers: 301 participants. Model AUC 0.751 (GPT-3.5) and 0.746 (PaLM2) on multiple choice, 0.781 (GPT-4o) short answer; human AUC with default explanations 0.589, 0.602 and 0.592. ECE example: model 0.104, human default 0.291, human modified 0.225.
quote: users tend to overestimate the accuracy of LLM responses when provided with default explanations
limits: Human reader study, not the model's own monitoring. Questions where participants lacked expertise. Multiple-choice models were overconfident, short-answer GPT-4o somewhat underconfident.
agent_relevance: Fluent, long output inflates trust in readers. A model judging its own long text may be fooled the same way (fluency cue). Judge short, length-normalised answers (G5).

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What Large Language Models Know and What People Think They Know
finding: Longer explanations raise human confidence without raising accuracy of judgement. This is a fluency illusion on LLM output.
numbers: Long explanations gave more confidence than short (Bayes factor 25) and short more than uncertainty-only (BF over 100). Human AUC 0.54 for long and 0.57 for uncertainty-only explanations (BF 0.23 for no difference).
quote: longer explanations increased user confidence, even when the extra length did not improve answer accuracy
limits: Pooled across Experiments 2a, 2b, 2c; small crowd samples.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G5: verbosity bias. Confidence taken from a judge should be normalised for length.

source: Gignac and Zajenkowski (2020) The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact (Intelligence 80)
finding: The classic quartile plot gives a Dunning-Kruger pattern in real data, but proper tests (heteroscedasticity and nonlinear regression) do not. The pattern is produced by the better-than-average effect plus regression to the mean.
numbers: N = 929 community adults, Raven's APM vs self-rated IQ. Self-rated 123.76 vs measured 101.70 (d = 1.71); r = 0.28. Quartile gaps 32.63, 22.05, 20.15, 12.68 (ANOVA F(3,925) = 79.00, eta-squared 0.20), yet no significant heteroscedasticity and an essentially linear relation.
quote: the association between objectively measured intelligence and self-assessed intelligence was found to be essentially entirely linear
limits: One skill (intelligence), one sample from Poland, a coarse 25-point self-rating. Absence of significance is not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Beware reading 'the weak are least aware' from quartile plots of any agent data. Estimate monitoring with within-model resolution and calibration, not by splitting on difficulty.

source: Dunkel, Nedelec and van der Linden (2023) Reevaluating the Dunning-Kruger effect: A response to and replication of Gignac and Zajenkowski (2020)
finding: With a large representative sample and the same unconfounded tests, a statistically significant but very small Dunning-Kruger effect appears.
numbers: N = 13,977 (AddHealth, ages 18 to 28). Self-assessed IQ below measured IQ on average (d = -0.14); r = 0.24; absolute residuals vs IQ r = -0.07; quadratic delta R2 = 0.011; cubic delta R2 = 0.001.
quote: our analyses illustrated a statistically significant DK effect. However, the magnitude of the effect was minimal
limits: Sample of young adults and a verbal-IQ type measure; self-assessment measure differs. Large N makes tiny effects significant.
agent_relevance: Net: the 'unskilled are unaware' claim is small after correcting artefacts. For the agent, do not expect a clear sign that weak answers come with weaker monitoring beyond what resolution already shows.

source: Healy and Moore (2007) Bayesian Overconfidence
finding: The hard-easy effect is explained by one Bayesian model without a special bias. People start with a guess of task difficulty. After an easy task they underestimate their score and overplace themselves; after a hard task they overestimate and underplace themselves.
numbers: 82 undergraduates, 10-item trivia quizzes of easy, medium and difficult sets, incentive-compatible belief reports. Interim overplacement 0.39 points after easy quizzes; underplacement 1.66 points after difficult quizzes; scores on easy vs difficult quizzes differ (z = 22.83).
quote: Task difficulty is negatively correlated with overestimation but positively correlated with overplacement.
limits: One lab experiment with students and trivia; model assumes simple Bayesian updating. It shows the effect can be rational, not that human confidence is optimal.
agent_relevance: Calibration should be judged within difficulty strata and against a task-difficulty prior. An agent that knows the base rate of success for a task type can correct hard-easy drift in code.

source: Gangemi, Bourgeois-Gironde and Mancini (2015) Feelings of error in reasoning: in search of a phenomenon
finding: People who give the intuitive wrong answer to the bat-and-ball problem report much more cognitive uneasiness than people who answer correctly or who solve the control version. So there is a feeling that tracks error, not only a feeling of rightness.
numbers: Study 1: N = 145 psychology undergraduates, 30% solved the standard problem, 97% the control. Uneasiness higher for standard vs control: F(1,101) = 658.46, partial eta-squared .87. Wrong 16.52 vs correct 8.79 (t(143) = 8.8). Study 2: N about 148, 34% correct; wrong 14.18 vs correct 11.37.
quote: it is diagnostic of genuine error
limits: Questionnaire filled after solving, so it can be retrospective rationalisation. Italian students; a single reasoning problem family. Study 2 (choice between two answers) narrows the gap.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that a conflict signal exists even when the answer is wrong, but only if conflict is measured (e.g. disagreement between two routes). In our agent: compute the conflict in code instead of asking.

source: Do LLMs Know What They Know? Measuring Metacognitive Efficiency with Signal Detection Theory (2026), arXiv 2603.25112
finding: Calibration scores (ECE, Brier) mix up how much a model knows with how well its confidence tracks knowledge. A signal-detection measure of metacognitive information varies about two-fold across models and is not predicted by accuracy.
numbers: Four LLMs, 224,000 factual QA trials (TriviaQA, Natural Questions). Metacognitive information varies by a factor of 1.98; rank correlation with accuracy -0.80 (TriviaQA) and +0.00 (NQ); z-ROC slopes 0.78 to 1.18. In v3 the earlier inverse accuracy-efficiency link failed after a length bias in the automatic correctness scorer was fixed (1,830 human checks).
limits: Read the abstract page only. Unreviewed preprint; one revision reversed an earlier claim; token log-probability is the confidence signal; models are not named in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Calibration and resolution are separate, so report both. Also a warning: the grading of correctness can bias monitoring results, so check any judge for length bias.

source: Merkle (2009) The disutility of the hard-easy effect in choice confidence (Psychonomic Bulletin and Review 16)
finding: Seen only as an abstract in search results. It derives the conditions for a hard-easy effect and argues that almost any judge shows it in realistic situations, so the effect cannot tell models of confidence apart.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; abstract-level summary from a search snippet only.
agent_relevance: Suggests the hard-easy effect is a weak test between theories; do not use it to choose a monitoring design.

source: Rhodes and Tauber (2011) The influence of delaying judgments of learning on metacognitive accuracy: a meta-analytic review (Psychological Bulletin 137)
finding: Confirmed by search that this meta-analysis exists and that delayed judgments of learning predict later recall better than immediate ones. I could not open the paper or confirm the gamma values.
numbers: None verified.
limits: Closed access; not opened. Do not quote numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: The delayed-JOL effect is the best human case that monitoring improves with a gap: judging after a break uses retrieval from memory instead of a fresh fluency cue. Agent analogue: judge an answer from a fresh context, not the context that produced it. Test this.

source: Wang and Thompson (2019) and Stewart thesis, Waterloo: Speed of response does not affect feelings of rightness in reasoning
finding: From the search snippet only: Feeling of rightness predicts later answer change, answer fluency is argued to drive it, and a manipulation of response execution did not affect it.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened; abstract-level snippet. Source attribution unclear (thesis page and a 2019 paper both appeared).
agent_relevance: If the feeling of rightness comes from answer fluency, an agent's first-pass confidence is a fluency cue, and a re-check should be triggered by code signals rather than by that feeling (G1).

source: Fleming and Lau (2014) How to measure metacognition (Frontiers in Human Neuroscience)
finding: Search snippets only: separates metacognitive bias, sensitivity and efficiency. Efficiency (meta-d' over d', the M-ratio) says how much of the available first-order information the confidence uses.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened. meta-d' is defined for two-choice detection; per the 2026 LLM paper it does not transfer cleanly to open-ended QA.
agent_relevance: Name the three quantities in our log: bias (average confidence minus accuracy), sensitivity (AUROC) and efficiency (sensitivity relative to what the task allowed).

source: Rahnev (2024) comparison of 17 measures of metacognition
finding: Search snippet only: 17 measures of metacognition were compared, including meta-d' and M-ratio, and all were found valid with differing precision.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened; the download failed in this session.
agent_relevance: Pick one resolution and one calibration measure up front and keep them fixed across our experiments.
